instruction: Why does someone keep coming to check on me when I'm sleeping?
response: That's your nurse! Nurses come to check on you during the night to make sure you're comfortable and safe. They might look at a machine near your bed, feel your forehead, or just peek in quietly. They try really hard not to wake you up. It's kind of like how your mom or dad might check on you at home before they go to bed — except nurses do it a few times during the night because that's their special job. If the light or sounds bother you, you can tell your nurse and they'll try to be extra quiet.

instruction: What's the bracelet they put on my arm?
response: That's your hospital armband! It has your name, your birthday, and a special barcode on it. Every time a nurse or doctor needs to give you medicine or do a test, they'll look at your bracelet to make absolutely sure they have the right kid. You might notice they ask your name and birthday a lot too — that's not because they forgot, it's another way they double-check so you stay safe. You need to keep it on the whole time you're here, but if it feels itchy or too tight, tell your nurse and they can fix it for you.

instruction: I'm hungry. When do I get food?
response: Meals come at set times here at the hospital. Breakfast arrives in the morning, lunch comes around noon, and dinner shows up in the late afternoon. Before your meal, you'll get a little form on your breakfast tray where you can pick what you'd like to eat the next day — kind of like ordering from a menu! But here's one important thing: before you eat or drink anything, your nurse needs to say it's okay. Sometimes doctors need your tummy to be empty for a test or procedure. If you're feeling really hungry between meals, ask your parent to check with your nurse about a snack.

instruction: Can my dog come visit me?
response: I know you must miss your dog a lot! Unfortunately, family pets usually aren't allowed to visit because the hospital needs to keep all the kids here safe and healthy. But there is some good news — the hospital has special therapy dogs that sometimes visit kids on certain units. These are friendly, trained dogs from St. John Ambulance who come just to cheer you up! Ask your parent to check with your care team about when the next therapy dog visit might happen. In the meantime, you could bring a photo of your dog or even a stuffed animal that reminds you of them.

instruction: There's a sign on my door and people keep putting on gowns. Am I in trouble?
response: You are definitely not in trouble! That sign means the doctors and nurses are being extra careful to stop germs from spreading. Sometimes when a kid is sick with something that could be passed on, the hospital puts up a sign so everyone remembers to put on special gloves, a gown, or a mask before they come in. It's kind of like putting on a raincoat to keep the rain off — the gown keeps germs from going in or out of the room. Your visitors will need to follow those rules too, but your nurse can show them exactly what to do. It's all about keeping everyone safe.

instruction: My room number is B2-503. What does that mean?
response: Your room number is like a little code that helps everyone find you! Let me break it down: the 'B' means you're in Zone B of the hospital — that's where Children's Hospital is. The '2' means you're on the second floor. And '503' is your actual room number on that floor. So if someone says 'B2-503,' they know exactly which building, which floor, and which room to go to. Pretty cool, right? It's kind of like how your home address has a street name and a house number so people can find where you live.

instruction: Why are they putting cream on my arm before the needle?
response: That cream is something really helpful — it's called a numbing cream! The nurses put it on your skin before a needle so that the spot gets kind of sleepy. When the cream does its job, you feel way less of the poke. This is part of something the hospital calls the Comfort Promise, which means they try really hard to make needles hurt as little as possible for every kid. They might also help you sit in a comfy position or let you watch a video or play with something while it happens. If you're feeling scared, it's totally okay to tell your nurse and they'll help you feel better.

instruction: Can I watch TV or play games here?
response: Yes! The hospital has a special entertainment website where you can watch live TV for free. If your family has a streaming account — like for movies or shows — you can log in and watch your favourite stuff too. There are also some really fun rooms to visit. The School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor has crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO. It's open during the day and sometimes the Child Life team runs special activities there. There's also a cool room called the SMILE Room that has bubble lights, music, and fibre optics — it's a really neat place to relax.

instruction: Why can't I bring my balloon into the hospital?
response: I know balloons are fun, but the hospital doesn't allow the regular rubbery kind — those are called latex balloons. Some people are really allergic to latex, and it can make them very sick, even if they just breathe near it. So to keep all the kids safe, those balloons have to stay outside. The good news is that foil balloons — the shiny, crinkly kind — are totally fine! So if someone wants to bring you a balloon to make your room cheerful, just let them know to get a foil one instead.

instruction: What happens when I get to go home? Do I just leave?
response: Not quite — but it's exciting news when the doctor says you're ready! Before you leave, your care team will sit down with your parent or guardian and go over everything: what medicines you'll need to take at home, when to come back for a check-up, and what to watch for. Your nurse will make sure your parent has written instructions so nobody has to remember it all in their head. You'll also need your car seat for the ride home — that's the law to keep you safe. Make sure you and your family pack up all your toys and belongings so nothing gets left behind!

instruction: I just got admitted. What's the deal with visiting hours and can my friends come see me?
response: Children's Hospital doesn't have one strict visiting schedule that applies to everyone — it depends on which unit you're on, your condition, and what your care team thinks is best. Generally, up to two care partners can be at your bedside at a time for inpatients. Your friends can visit, but it's worth checking with your unit's staff first about the best times. Visitors are asked to stay away if they've been sick in the past week, and everyone needs to wash their hands or use the hand sanitizer when they arrive and leave. Between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m., anyone staying with you is asked to remain in your room and let the staff know when they come and go.

instruction: I'm worried about privacy. Can the hospital tell anyone about my medical stuff?
response: Your privacy is taken seriously here. The hospital can only share information about your care with your parent or legal guardian — not friends, extended family, or anyone else without proper consent. If your family wants to keep everyone in the loop, one tip is to pick a single family contact person who can pass along updates. You also have rights around your personal health information, including the right to know who's accessed it and to request corrections if something's wrong. If you ever feel like your privacy isn't being respected, you or your parent can contact the Privacy Office at extension 32996 or email them directly.

instruction: What's the Wi-Fi situation here? Can I use my phone?
response: You're welcome to use your cell phone during your stay — the hospital actually encourages it so you can keep in touch with friends and family. There's Wi-Fi available on site; if you run into connection issues, there's a Data Valet helpline you can call at 1-800-642-3958. Patient phones are also available in rooms for local and toll-free calls at no charge. On top of that, there's an entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free or log in to your own streaming accounts. Just keep in mind that if you're on a unit with specific infection control rules, your care team might have guidelines about cleaning your devices.

instruction: I'm going to be here for a while. What is there to actually do in this hospital?
response: More than you'd expect. There's an activity room on B6 with games, crafts, and LEGO that's open during the day. The SMILE Room on the sixth floor is a sensory space with bubble columns, fibre optics, and music — good for when you need to decompress. If you're into creative expression, the hospital has both art therapy and music therapy programs. There's also the Heroes' Circle, which teaches breathing techniques and martial arts. If you're between 8 and 18, you can sign up for Upopolis, a secure social network that connects young patients across Canada — ask a Child Life Specialist for a laptop. And therapy dog visits happen on certain units, so check with your care team about the schedule.

instruction: The nurse mentioned a 'bedside shift change report.' What is that and do I have to be involved?
response: It's when the nurse finishing their shift hands off your care to the nurse starting the next one, and they do it right at your bedside instead of behind a desk. It typically takes about three to five minutes. The incoming nurse will introduce themselves, they'll review your plan of care together, run through safety checks, and then ask if you or your family have any questions or anything to add. You're encouraged to participate as much or as little as you want — it's your chance to correct anything that sounds off or bring up something you've noticed. Before they leave, your nurse will let you know when to expect them back.

instruction: What kind of food options are there? I'm vegetarian.
response: The hospital offers a range of dietary options including vegetarian, vegan, halal, kosher, and allergy-specific diets. When you're admitted, let your care team know you're vegetarian and they'll make sure your meals reflect that. Each day, a menu form comes on your breakfast tray so you can choose what you'd like for the next day's meals. Breakfast is served around 7:45–8:45 a.m., lunch around 11:45 a.m.–12:45 p.m., and dinner around 4:45–5:45 p.m. If you need something between meals, the inpatient pantries on B6 have drinks and light snacks. There's also an On the Go featuring Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B, open weekdays from 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. — though it's closed on weekends.

instruction: I'm nervous about having a needle procedure tomorrow. What do they do to make it easier?
response: The hospital has something called the Comfort Promise, which is their commitment to minimizing pain and anxiety around needles for every patient. For someone your age, that typically includes a topical numbing cream or gel applied to your skin beforehand so the poke is much less intense. They'll also use comfort positioning — sitting upright in a secure, supported position rather than being held down, which evidence shows makes a real difference. Distraction techniques are another option, like watching something on your phone or focusing on music. You can ask about any of these before your procedure, and your care team will work with you to figure out what combination helps most.

instruction: I'm 16 and I've been told I'll eventually transfer to adult care. What does that even look like?
response: That's a really valid thing to be thinking about. Children's Hospital has a Transitions in Care team whose whole job is to help patients and families navigate big milestones like moving from paediatric to adult care. They work with you ahead of time so it's not a sudden switch — it's more of a gradual process where you build the skills and knowledge to manage your own health care. They can also help with the transition between school and hospital if you've been missing classes. The best first step is to bring it up with your care team or ask to connect with the Transitions in Care team directly so you know what the timeline and plan look like for your specific situation.

instruction: What happens with security here? I noticed some kind of scanner at the emergency entrance.
response: The hospital uses a weapons detection system at the Emergency Department entrances. Everyone entering the ED walks through it each time, including young patients — though minors are always scanned with a parent or guardian present. The technology is non-invasive, so you don't need to stop, empty your pockets, or remove anything. It works as you walk through. If the system flags something, a trained security guard may check your belongings. There are accommodations for people who can't go through the standard way, so if you need an alternative, talk to the security guard at the entrance before going in. Outside the ED, the main B Tower entrance is open from 6 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. and access is controlled by security after hours.

instruction: I'm kind of stressed about all of this. Is there anyone I can talk to who isn't my doctor or my parents?
response: Absolutely. There are several people you can connect with. Child Life Specialists are trained specifically to help young people cope with the stress of being in the hospital — they're not doctors, and talking to them is more informal. Social workers are also available and can offer emotional support, help with practical stuff, and connect you with community resources. If you'd find it helpful, there's a Paediatric Psychology service for patients dealing with adjustment challenges. For something more reflective or spiritual, there's a Spiritual Care team available to everyone regardless of beliefs, and a Sanctuary space on the third floor of Zone C that's open 24/7 for quiet time. Ask your nurse to connect you with whoever feels like the right fit.
